title: Unit 4d - Double-Ended Queues (Deques) Introduction
summary: Title slide introducing the Deques unit in CS 103, covering double-ended queue data structures and their implementations. Presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 4d on Double-Ended Queues (Deques) in the CS 103 course. A deque is a data structure that supports fast insertion and removal from both the front and back. This unit covers the motivation for deques, explores different possible implementations using singly-linked lists, doubly-linked lists, and arrays, and introduces the C++ deque class from the Standard Template Library.
notes_text: Deques are pronounced like 'deck' and the name comes from 'double-ended queue'. They are an important abstract data type that bridges the gap between stacks and queues.

title: Singly-Linked List Review
summary: Reviews singly-linked lists: each node has a value and next pointer, traversal is only forward, and you cannot recover the previous item from a given node.
main_text: Singly-linked lists use structures/classes and pointers to make linked data structures. They dynamically allocate each item when the user decides to add it. Each item includes a next pointer to the following item. Traversal and iteration is only easily achieved in one direction (the forward direction). The Item struct contains an int val and an Item* next pointer. The List class has a constructor, destructor, push_back method, and a private Item* head member. In the diagram, head points to the first node (value 3 at address 0x148), which points to the next node (value 9 at address 0x1c0), which points to the last node (value 2 at address 0x164) with next=NULL. An important question is posed: given a temp pointer to the middle node, could you ever recover the address of the previous item? The answer is No, because singly-linked lists only have forward pointers.
notes_text: The inability to go backwards in a singly-linked list is the key limitation that motivates doubly-linked lists. This becomes critical when trying to implement a deque, where we need to remove from the back efficiently.

images.description: Diagram showing a singly-linked list with three nodes: node at 0x148 (val=3, next=0x1c0), node at 0x1c0 (val=9, next=0x164), and node at 0x164 (val=2, next=NULL). Head pointer and temp pointer are shown, with a question about recovering the previous node answered with 'No!!!'.

title: Doubly-Linked Lists
summary: Introduces doubly-linked lists where each node has both a previous and next pointer, enabling bidirectional traversal.
main_text: A doubly-linked list includes a previous pointer in each item so that we can traverse/iterate backwards or forward. The DLItem struct contains int val, DLItem* prev, and DLItem* next. The first item's previous field should be NULL, and the last item's next field should be NULL. The DLList class has a constructor, destructor, push_back method, and a private DLItem* head member. In the diagram, head points to address 0x148. The first node (val=3) has prev=NULL and next=0x1c0. The second node (val=9, at 0x1c0) has prev=0x148 and next=0x210. The third node (val=5, at 0x210) has prev=0x1c0 and next=NULL. Each node's blueprint shows three fields: DLItem* prev, int val, and DLItem* next, making each node larger than a singly-linked list node but enabling bidirectional traversal.
notes_text: Doubly-linked lists trade memory (extra pointer per node) for the ability to traverse in both directions. This is essential for efficient removal from the back of the list, which is needed for deque implementation.

images.description: Diagram showing a doubly-linked list with three nodes connected by forward and backward pointers. Each node has prev, val, and next fields. Node at 0x148 (val=3, prev=NULL), node at 0x1c0 (val=9), and node at 0x210 (val=5, next=NULL). A blueprint shows the DLItem structure with three fields.

title: Deques and Their Implementation Section Divider
summary: Section divider transitioning to the topic of using a doubly-linked list to implement a deque.
main_text: This is a section divider slide marking the transition to the topic of Deques and Their Implementation. The subtitle indicates the focus will be on using a doubly-linked list to implement a deque. This section explores different linked list configurations and analyzes which ones can achieve the O(1) insertion and removal from both ends that defines a deque.
notes_text: The exploration of different implementation strategies (singly-linked with/without tail, doubly-linked with tail) builds understanding of why certain design choices are necessary.

title: Deques Definition and Operations
summary: Defines a deque as a data structure allowing O(1) insertion and removal from both front and back, with push_front, pop_front, push_back, and pop_back operations.
main_text: A Double-ended queue (deque, like the name sounds: 'D-que') is the name given to any data structure that allows fast (O(1)) insertion and removal from BOTH SIDES (front and back) of the list. The four core operations are: push_front() at O(1), push_back() at O(1), pop_front() at O(1), and pop_back() at O(1). There are several possible implementations of such a data structure. The key requirement is that all four operations must be constant time O(1). The diagram shows a deque as a box with arrows indicating push_front and pop_front on the left side, and push_back and pop_back on the right side, all labeled O(1). The text notes that many possible implementations exist for this abstract data type.
notes_text: A deque is an abstract data type defined by its interface (the four O(1) operations), not by its implementation. This means any data structure that achieves these time complexities qualifies as a deque implementation. The name is a portmanteau of 'double-ended queue'.

images.description: Diagram showing a deque as an orange box labeled 'Deque (Many possible implementations exist)' with arrows on the left for push_front O(1) entering and pop_front O(1) exiting, and arrows on the right for push_back O(1) entering and pop_back O(1) exiting.

title: Can A Vector Be a Deque
summary: Asks whether a vector (array) can serve as a deque implementation by achieving O(1) add/remove from both front and back. The answer is no.
main_text: This slide poses the question: can an array add/remove from the front and back in O(1)? The operations are listed with blank complexities for students to fill in: push_front() O(?), push_back() O(?), pop_front() O(?), pop_back() O(?). While push_back and pop_back can be O(1) for a vector, push_front and pop_front require shifting all elements, making them O(n). Therefore, a vector cannot serve as a deque. The diagram shows a deque box containing array elements [51, 71, 28, 10] with arrows for all four operations labeled O(1), but this is the target behavior that a plain vector cannot achieve.
notes_text: This is a key conceptual question. Vectors are fast at the back (O(1) amortized for push_back, O(1) for pop_back) but slow at the front (O(n) for both push_front and pop_front due to element shifting). This motivates looking at linked-list-based implementations.

images.description: Diagram showing a deque box with array elements [51, 71, 28, 10] inside, with arrows for push_front O(1), pop_front O(1), push_back O(1), and pop_back O(1) representing the ideal deque interface.

title: Deque Implementations Overview
summary: States that while a vector cannot be a deque, several implementations exist including linked-list based and C++ array-based deque implementations.
main_text: While a vector cannot be a deque, there are several possible implementations of such a data structure. The course will first explore a linked-list implementation for a deque, then note that C++ also provides an array-based deque implementation. The diagram shows a deque with push_front and pop_front arrows on the left, and push_back and pop_back arrows on the right, with linked list nodes visible inside the deque container, suggesting the linked-list implementation approach. The nodes are connected with bidirectional arrows indicating a doubly-linked structure.
notes_text: The two main approaches to implementing a deque are: (1) linked-list based, which is explored in detail in this unit, and (2) array-based using a circular buffer, which the C++ STL deque class uses internally.

images.description: Diagram showing a deque container with linked list nodes inside, connected by bidirectional arrows. Push_front and pop_front arrows on the left, push_back and pop_back arrows on the right.

title: Deque Implementation - Exploration Question
summary: Poses the question of whether a singly-linked list can achieve O(1) insertion/removal from both front and back, and sets up analysis of different implementations.
main_text: This slide sets up the exploration of deque implementation. The key question for exploration is: could we use a singly-linked list and still get fast (O(1)) insertion/removal from both front and back? For various implementations, students should analyze the runtime for each operation: push_front(), pop_front(), push_back(), and pop_back(). This systematic analysis will reveal which linked list configurations can and cannot serve as deques, building understanding of why certain design choices are necessary.
notes_text: The approach of analyzing each operation's complexity for different data structure configurations is a fundamental technique in computer science. It helps students understand the trade-offs between different implementations.

title: Singly-Linked List Deque Analysis
summary: Analyzes singly-linked list operations for deque suitability, asking students to determine O(1) vs O(n) complexity for push_front, pop_front, push_back, and pop_back.
main_text: With a singly-linked list (head pointer only), which operations are O(1) vs O(n)? The four operations are listed with blank complexities for students to fill in: push_front() O(?), pop_front() O(?), push_back() O(?), pop_back() O(?). With only a head pointer, push_front is O(1) because we just create a new node and point it to the current head. pop_front is O(1) because we just move head to head->next and delete the old head. However, push_back is O(n) because we must traverse to the end to add a node, and pop_back is O(n) because we must traverse to find the second-to-last node. The diagram shows the linked list: head at 0x148 pointing to node (val=3) -> node (val=9) -> node (val=2, next=NULL).
notes_text: A basic singly-linked list with only a head pointer fails the deque requirements because back operations require traversing the entire list. This motivates adding a tail pointer to speed up back operations.

images.description: Singly-linked list diagram with head pointer at 0x148, three nodes: (3, 0x1c0), (9, 0x164), (2, NULL). Shows the basic structure being analyzed for deque operation complexities.

title: Singly-Linked List With Tail Pointer - Push Back Analysis
summary: Adding a tail pointer to a singly-linked list makes push_front O(1), pop_front O(1), and push_back O(1), but leaves push_back's complexity as a question.
main_text: Suppose we keep a second pointer (a tail pointer) to always point at the LAST element. The head points at the FIRST element and tail points at the LAST element. With this configuration, which operations are O(1) vs O(n)? push_front() is O(1) and pop_front() is O(1), same as before since we still have the head pointer. push_back() complexity is left as a question for students. With a tail pointer, push_back becomes O(1) because we can directly access the last node through the tail pointer, create a new node, set the old tail's next to the new node, and update tail to the new node. The diagram shows head at 0x148 and tail at 0x164, with the linked list: node (val=3) -> node (val=9) -> node (val=2, next=NULL).
notes_text: The tail pointer solves the push_back problem by giving direct access to the end of the list. However, pop_back still requires finding the second-to-last node, which the tail pointer alone cannot provide in a singly-linked list.

images.description: Singly-linked list with both head (0x148) and tail (0x164) pointers. Three nodes: (3) -> (9) -> (2, NULL). Tail pointer points directly to the last node, enabling O(1) push_back.

title: Singly-Linked List With Tail Pointer - Pop Back Analysis
summary: Shows that even with a tail pointer, pop_back remains a question because removing the last element requires finding the second-to-last node.
main_text: Continuing the analysis of a singly-linked list with tail pointer: push_front() is O(1), pop_front() is O(1), push_back() is O(1) thanks to the tail pointer. But pop_back() complexity is left as a question. The diagram now shows four nodes: head at 0x148 pointing to node (val=3) -> node (val=9, at 0x290) -> node (val=9, at 0x1c0) -> node (val=2 at 0x164, next=NULL), with tail pointing to the last node. The challenge with pop_back is that after removing the last node, we need to update the tail to point to the second-to-last node, and in a singly-linked list we have no way to find that node without traversing from the head.
notes_text: Even though we know where the tail is, we cannot move backwards in a singly-linked list. To pop_back, we must traverse from head to find the node whose next pointer equals tail, making it O(n). This is the fundamental limitation.

images.description: Singly-linked list with head and tail pointers, showing four nodes connected by next pointers. The challenge of pop_back is implied: after removing the tail node, how do we update the tail pointer?

title: Singly-Linked List Cannot Remove From Back in O(1)
summary: Concludes that even with a tail pointer, a singly-linked list CANNOT pop_back in O(1) because finding the second-to-last node requires traversal.
main_text: The complete analysis of singly-linked lists with tail pointer shows: push_front() is O(1), pop_front() is O(1), push_back() is O(1), but pop_back() is O(n). So even with a tail pointer, a singly-linked list CANNOT remove from the back in O(1). The reason is that we have to update the second-to-last item (make it the new tail and set its next to NULL), and we cannot find that item quickly without walking the entire list from the head. Since pop_back is O(n), a singly-linked list with tail pointer does not meet the deque requirement of all four operations being O(1).
notes_text: This is a critical insight: the singly-linked list's inability to move backwards means pop_back will always be O(n) regardless of what additional pointers we maintain. The solution requires each node to store a pointer to its predecessor, which leads to the doubly-linked list.

images.description: Singly-linked list with head and tail pointers showing four nodes. Pop_back is highlighted as O(n) in red/pink, demonstrating the fundamental limitation of singly-linked lists for deque implementation.

title: Doubly-Linked List With Tail Pointer - Setup
summary: Proposes using a doubly-linked list with tail pointer to achieve O(1) for all deque operations, since the prev pointer allows moving backwards.
main_text: Since removal from the back needs to move the tail BACK 1 step to the previous item, the solution is to use a doubly-linked list. With a doubly-linked list and tail pointer: push_front() is O(1), pop_front() is O(1), push_back() is O(1), and pop_back() complexity is left as a question. The diagram shows head at 0x148 and tail at 0x210, with four doubly-linked nodes: node at 0x148 (val=3, prev=NULL, next=0x190), node at 0x190 (val=12, prev=0x148, next=0x1c0), node at 0x1c0 (val=9, prev=0x190, next=0x210), node at 0x210 (val=5, prev=0x1c0, next=NULL). Each node has prev, val, and next fields connected bidirectionally.
notes_text: The doubly-linked list with tail pointer is the key insight. Because each node has a prev pointer, we can access the second-to-last node in O(1) via tail->prev, which is exactly what we need for efficient pop_back.

images.description: Doubly-linked list with head and tail pointers, showing four nodes with prev, val, and next fields. Bidirectional arrows connect consecutive nodes. Head points to first node (val=3) and tail points to last node (val=5).

title: Doubly-Linked List With Tail Pointer - Pop Back is O(1)
summary: Shows that pop_back is O(1) with a doubly-linked list because tail = tail->prev gives direct access to the second-to-last node.
main_text: With a doubly-linked list and tail pointer, all four operations are O(1): push_front() O(1), pop_front() O(1), push_back() O(1), and pop_back() O(1). We can update the tail pointer with the tail item's previous pointer before we delete the tail item, using the expression: tail = tail->prev. The diagram shows the pop_back process: the tail pointer (originally at 0x210 pointing to node val=5) is updated to 0x1c0 (the node with val=9). The node at 0x1c0 has its next pointer set to NULL (shown as 0x0), and the old tail node (val=5) is crossed out with a prohibition sign indicating it will be deleted. The key operation is that tail->prev gives us the second-to-last node in O(1), which was impossible with a singly-linked list.
notes_text: The complete pop_back algorithm is: (1) save tail->prev as the new tail, (2) set the new tail's next to NULL, (3) delete the old tail node, (4) update the tail pointer. All of these are O(1) operations because we have direct pointer access.

images.description: Doubly-linked list showing the pop_back operation. Tail pointer moves from node at 0x210 (val=5, crossed out) back to node at 0x1c0 (val=9). The expression 'tail = tail->prev;' is shown. Node at 0x1c0 has its next updated to 0x0 (NULL).

title: Success - Doubly-Linked List Deque Implementation
summary: Confirms that a doubly-linked list with tail pointer achieves O(1) for all four deque operations, while a singly-linked list cannot.
main_text: We have successfully found a deque implementation. We can insert and remove from the front or back quickly (in O(1)). The final analysis: push_front() O(1), pop_front() O(1), push_back() O(1), pop_back() O(1). The key conclusions are: a singly-linked list CANNOT serve as a deque because pop_back requires O(n) traversal, but a double-linked list with tail pointer CAN serve as a deque because the prev pointers allow O(1) access to the previous node. The diagram shows the complete doubly-linked list with head at 0x148 and tail at 0x210, with four nodes (val=3, 12, 9, 5) connected bidirectionally with prev and next pointers.
notes_text: This is the culmination of the implementation exploration. The doubly-linked list with tail pointer satisfies all deque requirements. The extra memory cost of prev pointers and the tail pointer is the trade-off for achieving O(1) on all operations.

images.description: Complete doubly-linked list deque implementation showing four nodes with bidirectional connections. Head and tail pointers provide O(1) access to both ends. All four deque operations listed as O(1).

title: A Thought Experiment - Eliminating the Tail Pointer
summary: Asks whether O(1) insert and removal from the end can be achieved without a tail pointer, by restructuring the linked list.
main_text: This slide poses a thought experiment: do we really need the tail pointer to achieve O(1) insert and removal from the end? Seemingly yes, because how else would we know where the end is? The deeper question is: is there a way we could structure our linked list to make finding the last item easy and fast but by only using a head pointer? The diagram shows the same doubly-linked list but with the tail pointer crossed out with a prohibition sign, leaving only the head pointer. The four nodes (val=3, 12, 9, 5) are still connected bidirectionally. This sets up the circular linked list concept on the next slide.
notes_text: This thought experiment leads students to discover the circular linked list concept on their own. By having the last node's next point back to the first node and the first node's prev point to the last node, we can find the tail via head->prev in O(1).

images.description: Doubly-linked list with the tail pointer crossed out (prohibition sign), leaving only the head pointer. Four nodes connected bidirectionally. Poses the question of how to access the end without a tail pointer.

title: Circular Linked List
summary: Introduces circular linked lists where the first and last nodes point to each other, eliminating the need for a tail pointer since head->prev gives the tail.
main_text: Though there is no great benefit over just using a tail pointer, we can implement a deque as a doubly-linked list with only a head pointer by making the first and last item point at each other. This effectively creates a circular linked list. The question is posed: what expression would yield a pointer to the tail item? The answer (left blank for students) is head->prev. It saves a pointer, but is harder to code/implement, so the recommendation is to just stick with the tail pointer implementation. The diagram shows head at 0x148, and four nodes: node at 0x148 (val=3, prev=0x210, next=0x190), node at 0x190 (val=12, prev=0x148, next=0x1c0), node at 0x1c0 (val=9, prev=0x190, next=0x210), node at 0x210 (val=5, prev=0x1c0, next=0x148). Note that the last node's next points back to the first node (0x148), and the first node's prev points to the last node (0x210), creating the circular structure.
notes_text: The circular linked list is an elegant alternative that eliminates the tail pointer. The expression head->prev gives O(1) access to the last node. However, the implementation is trickier because there are no NULL terminators to detect the end of the list, making traversal and edge cases more complex.

images.description: Circular doubly-linked list with only a head pointer. Four nodes connected in a circle: the last node (val=5) has next pointing back to the first node (val=3), and the first node has prev pointing to the last node. No NULL pointers exist.

title: C++ Deque Class Section Divider
summary: Section divider transitioning to the C++ deque class from the Standard Template Library.
main_text: This is a section divider slide marking the transition to the C++ Deque Class. After exploring linked-list-based deque implementations, the course now covers the actual C++ STL deque class, which provides a ready-to-use deque implementation with efficient operations on both ends.
notes_text: The C++ STL deque class uses an array-based implementation internally (not a linked list), which provides the additional benefit of random access, unlike a linked-list-based deque.

title: C++ Deque Class Usage
summary: Demonstrates the C++ deque class with code showing push_back, push_front, indexing, front/pop_front operations, and how elements shift during operations.
main_text: The C++ deque class has pros and cons compared to vector. Pros: Similar to vector but allows for efficient O(1) push_front() and pop_front() operations. Cons: Slightly slower random access (accessing the i-th element / data[i]). It is useful when we want to put things in one end of the list and take them out of the other. A complete code example demonstrates: (1) A loop pushes i+50 to the back and i to the front for i=0,1,2. After the first iteration, my_deq contains [0, 50]. After all iterations, my_deq contains [2, 1, 0, 50, 51, 52]. (2) Accessing my_deq[2] gives 0 (the element at index 2). (3) A loop moves front elements to back with +10: gets front value, pushes it+10 to back, then pops front. After this loop my_deq becomes [12, 11, 10, 60, 61, 62]. (4) A while loop prints and removes all elements from the front until empty.
notes_text: The deque class uses #include <deque> and deque<int> syntax. It supports all the same operations as vector (push_back, pop_back, front, back, size, empty, operator[]) plus push_front and pop_front. The pattern of pushing to one end and popping from the other is the classic queue pattern.

images.description: Four sequential states of the deque my_deq: (1) [0, 50] after first iteration, (2) [2, 1, 0, 50, 51, 52] after all iterations, (3) [12, 11, 10, 60, 61, 62] after the transfer loop, (4) empty after draining. Code shown on the right demonstrates all operations.

title: Array-Based Deque Implementation
summary: Explains how to implement a deque using a circular array with head and tail pointers, using modulo arithmetic to wrap around the array boundaries.
main_text: An array-based deque implementation works by taking an array but imagining it wrapping into a circle. Setup requires a head and tail pointer: head points at the first occupied item, and tail points at the first free location. Push_front() and pop_front() update the head pointer, while push_back() and pop_back() update the tail pointer. To overcome the discontinuity from index 0 to MAX-1 (wrapping around the array), use the modulo operation. You cannot just use back++ to move the back pointer; instead, use back = (back + 1) % MAX to wrap around correctly. Getting an item at index i must be relative to the front pointer, not absolute array position. The diagram shows an actual linear array with 8 slots (indices 0-7), then visualized as a circular array. Initially front and back point to the same location. After two push_back operations, size=2 and back has moved. After a push_front, size=3, front has moved counterclockwise, and back stays.
notes_text: The circular array approach is what the C++ STL deque uses internally (with some additional complexity involving multiple array chunks). The modulo trick ensures indices wrap around: after index MAX-1, the next index is 0. This gives O(1) for all four deque operations without linked list overhead.

images.description: Three views of array-based deque: (1) Linear array with 8 slots showing indices 0-7, (2) Same array visualized as a circle with indices 0-7 around the circumference, front and back pointers shown as green dots, (3) After push_back twice: size=2, back moved clockwise, (4) After push_front: size=3, front moved counterclockwise.

title: C++ Deque Class Performance
summary: Summarizes deque performance: slightly slower random access than vector, but fast O(1) addition and removal at both front and back.
main_text: The C++ deque class has the following performance characteristics: it is slightly slower at random access (array-style indexing access such as data[3]) than a vector. However, it is fast at adding or removing items at front or back, with all four operations (push_front, pop_front, push_back, pop_back) running in O(1) time. This makes the deque ideal for situations where you need efficient access to both ends of a collection, such as implementing queues, sliding window algorithms, or breadth-first search.
notes_text: The slight slowdown in random access compared to vectors comes from the deque's internal structure. While a vector stores all elements in a single contiguous array, a deque typically uses a series of fixed-size array blocks managed by a map/index structure, requiring an extra level of indirection for element access.

title: Deques Summary
summary: Summarizes that deques can be implemented with arrays or doubly-linked lists, implementation determines operation runtimes, and O(1) front/back access is the key guarantee.
main_text: Multiple possible implementations of deques exist: array-based (using circular buffer with modulo arithmetic) and doubly-linked list (recall a singly-linked list cannot pop_back() in O(1)). The implementation will determine the runtime of various operations. An important question is raised: can a doubly-linked list support O(1) access to a random element (i.e., can you access list[i] quickly for any i)? The answer is No! You still need to traverse the list to reach element i, making random access O(n). The only thing a deque guarantees is O(1) access to add/remove from either the front or back. Random access performance depends on the implementation: the C++ STL deque provides near-O(1) random access through its array-based approach, but a linked-list-based deque would have O(n) random access.
notes_text: The distinction between the abstract data type (deque with its O(1) front/back operations) and concrete implementations (array vs linked list) is fundamental to data structure design. Each implementation has trade-offs: linked lists offer true O(1) insert/remove but O(n) random access, while arrays offer near-O(1) random access with the complexity of circular buffer management.
